contradiction.viewer_thinks: you are skating on solid ice
contradiction.actually: you glide on a microscopic quasi-liquid water film on the ice surface

beats.narration: You can stand on a frozen lake, yet glide across it like glass. Why is ice slippery?
beats.claim: ice is slippery because of a thin near-surface water layer, not standing water
beats.visual_question: why is ice slippery at all?
beats.visual_answer: a bare frozen surface that already lets you glide, nothing added

beats.narration: The textbook answer blames pressure melting: the blade's weight squeezes meltwater out of the contact. But a skate lowers the melting point by only about 0.1 degrees.
beats.claim: the textbook blames pressure melting, but a skate lowers the melting point by only about 0.1 degrees
beats.visual_question: does a skate really melt the ice by pressing on it?
beats.visual_answer: a heavy downward pressure wedge squeezing meltwater out at the blade contact

beats.narration: Inside the ice, every water molecule grips four neighbours in open hexagonal rings.
beats.claim: inside the ice, every water molecule grips four neighbours in open hexagonal rings
beats.visual_question: what does the ice look like below the surface?
beats.visual_answer: nested hexagonal rings of water molecules gripping four neighbours, shrinking toward a glowing center

beats.narration: At the surface, molecules lose half their bonds and form a liquid film about 10 nanometers thick before any weight arrives.
beats.claim: at the surface, molecules lose half their bonds and form a liquid film about 10 nanometers thick before any weight arrives
beats.visual_question: where does the water come from if no one is pressing?
beats.visual_answer: the surface loses half its bonds and wears its own thin liquid film below freezing

beats.narration: The blade rides its own lubricant, and glide friction feeds the film faster than it can refreeze.
beats.claim: the blade rides its own lubricant, and glide friction feeds the film faster than it can refreeze
beats.visual_question: what keeps the film flowing while the blade moves?
beats.visual_answer: the blade edge rides and renews the film, friction feeding it faster than it refreezes

beats.narration: So ice is slippery — the leading explanation: it carries its own lubricant, a whisper of water at the surface, renewed by every glide.
beats.claim: ice is a solid that carries its own lubricant, renewed at every touch
beats.visual_answer: a solid that carries its own liquid skin — lattice below, glowing film above

visual_contradiction.actually: a microscopic interface of quasi-liquid water underneath
visual_contradiction.reveal: the camera enters the ice surface and the hidden lubricating layer becomes visible

payoff_image.image: the solid carrying its own liquid skin — hexagonal lattice rings beneath a thin glowing water film, one frame holds the whole mechanism
